report:
### Conclusion
Evidence suggests that acupuncture may help reduce depressive symptoms during pregnancy, but overall clinical data remain limited, leaving its efficacy inconclusive compared to standard treatments.

### Evidence For the Claim
A landmark randomized controlled trial of 150 pregnant women diagnosed with major depressive disorder found that 8 weeks of depression-specific acupuncture led to significantly greater symptom reduction and higher response rates than non-specific control acupuncture or massage therapy (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Fulltext/2010/03000/Acupuncture_for_Depression_During_Pregnancy__A.7.aspx). Small clinical and feasibility studies also report that acupuncture is a well-tolerated, non-pharmacological option with minimal risk of adverse events during pregnancy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10122233/).

### Evidence Against / Limitations
Despite these promising findings, the broader evidence base suffers from key limitations. Clinical trials focusing specifically on antenatal depression remain small and few in number. Comprehensive systematic reviews, such as those conducted by the Cochrane Collaboration, note that evidence regarding acupuncture for depression is overall inconsistent, varied in quality, and insufficient to draw firm conclusions or substitute established first-line treatments like psychotherapy (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004046_acupuncture-depression).

### Cited Sources
1. *Obstetrics & Gynecology* (2010 Trial): https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Fulltext/2010/03000/Acupuncture_for_Depression_During_Pregnancy__A.7.aspx
2. *PMC / Antenatal Depression Interventions*: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10122233/
3. *Cochrane Review on Acupuncture for Depression*: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004046_acupuncture-depression
